edges.effect_quant: In 1060 Thai children, serum retinol was significantly associated with hematocrit, serum iron, transferrin, ferritin, and transferrin saturation; in 919 Marshall Islands preschoolers, 59.9% had vitamin A deficiency, 53.5% had iron deficiency, and 33.2% had both; in 312 Brazilian children, higher retinol was associated with lower odds of anemia (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.29-0.59 as reported in the abstract).
edges.population: children in community, nutrition-transition, and malnutrition settings with low retinol or vitamin A deficiency
edges.mechanism: Vitamin A supports mobilization of iron from stores, erythropoiesis, epithelial integrity, and immune regulation. When retinol status is low, iron can be trapped in storage sites or diverted by inflammation, leaving children more prone to low serum iron, anemia, and combined micronutrient deficiency states.
edges.summary: Low vitamin A status in children tends to travel with poorer iron status and more anemia, and observational plus intervention-linked evidence support a biologically meaningful interaction between the two micronutrients. The relationship is not identical in every setting, but the overall direction is clearly unfavorable when vitamin A deficiency is present.
edges.caveats: Not all child trials show a strong ferritin response, and inflammation can distort both ferritin and retinol measurements. Some of the best evidence is from low-resource or malnutrition settings, so effect size may differ in healthier populations.
